title: The 10 Best Pneumatic Framing Nailers
subtitle: Air framing nailers for studs, decks, sheathing and fencing, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: A pneumatic framing nailer drives 2- to 3-1/2-inch nails for walls, decks, roof sheathing and fences. Most use 21-degree plastic-collated strips; some take 30-degree paper strips or 15-degree wire coils, and the angle decides which nails you can buy. We ranked 10 best-sellers on rating, review volume and features (selectable trigger, tool-free depth, dry-fire lockout and a rafter hook). They run from about $96 to $270. A framing nailer needs a compressor with around 2 to 4 CFM; see our air compressor list.

avoid.verdict: A 21-degree nailer whose listing disagrees with itself on weight, sold for about $43 more than what appears to be the same tool under the VEVOR name. The 3PLUS and NuMax picks cost less and are rated higher.

Its model number, RHF9021, matches the VEVOR framing nailer (RHF9021C), which sells for $96.90, so you'd pay about $43 extra for the AEROPRO label.
It's rated 3.8 stars, the lowest of the framing nailers we considered.

buyers_guide.q: 21°, 30° or 15° coil: which should I buy?
buyers_guide.a: The angle decides which nails fit. 21° plastic strips with full round heads are the most common and are accepted by building codes everywhere. 30° paper strips fit tighter corners but often use clipped or offset heads, which some codes don't allow. 15° coils hold the most nails and are popular for sheathing and subfloor.

buyers_guide.q: What size compressor does a framing nailer need?
buyers_guide.a: Plan on 2 to 4 CFM at 90 PSI for steady framing. A 6-gallon pancake handles one nailer at a casual pace; for fast framing or two guns, use a bigger tank with 4+ CFM. See our air compressor list.

Bump (contact) mode fires each time the nose hits with the trigger held, which is fast for sheathing and subfloor. Sequential mode is safer and more precise for framing members. A selectable trigger lets you choose.
It's a metal hook that lets you hang the nailer on a joist, rafter or ladder rung instead of setting it down. Pros working at height use it constantly.

Pneumatic nailers are lighter, cheaper and drive nails all day, but you drag a hose and run a compressor. Cordless framers are heavier and more expensive, but there's no setup. For lots of framing, pneumatic wins on cost and weight.
